{"id": "90:17/q13", "question": "Why single out patience and mercy as the believers' paired virtues?", "turns_on": "Whether the pair is read as religious foundations, cardinal virtues, a shared social ethic, or a contrast with the idolaters.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q13/p1", "position": "They gather duty toward God and care for creation, the foundations of obedience.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī describe patience as honoring God's command and mercy as compassion for creatures; cited investigators call sincerity with God and good character with people the foundations of Sufism. Ibn ʿĀshūr says all good deeds need restraint of desire and mercy sustains the community, comparing 48:29."}, {"id": "90:17/q13/p2", "position": "They complete a progression of four cardinal virtues: generosity or chastity, faith as wisdom, patience as courage, and mercy as justice.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says courage depends on certainty and each named trait stands for its broader virtue; al-Bursawī quotes a teacher who calls feeding in hardship supreme restraint, faith wisdom, patience courage and mercy justice. Al-Biqāʿī calls faith wisdom's second ascent, courage the third and mercy a fourth balanced pass."}, {"id": "90:17/q13/p3", "position": "They define a community that resists injustice with steadfastness and merciful solidarity.", "reasons": "Quṭb stresses collective mutual support alongside personal judgment; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says genuine faith bears struggle for good and refusal to stay silent about injustice. Kur'an Yolu identifies slavery, poverty and mercilessness as the era's grave problems; these duties are examples of Islamic social ethics, not an exhaustive list."}, {"id": "90:17/q13/p4", "position": "Their praise exposes the idolaters' lack of patience and compassion.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the indirect rebuke is explicit in passages on calling to God, patience, honoring orphans and feeding the poor: 41:33, 41:35, 89:17 and 89:18."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q14", "question": "How does this verse complete the account of crossing the obstacle?", "turns_on": "Whether the ascent is a set of acts requiring faith, a moral progression toward it, or a socially grounded sequence.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q14/p1", "position": "The earlier freeing and feeding are joined by faith, patience, and mercy as the complete route.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ counts the three parts under one negative. Al-Iṣlāḥī says bodily faculties and moral awareness in 8–17 should overcome greed and serve God. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the Qur'an itself defines the obstacle, rejecting a need for allegorical readings. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says the explicit deeds already replace the usual phrase 'righteous deeds' after faith; patience and mercy follow the difficult works."}, {"id": "90:17/q14/p2", "position": "The preceding social acts can show innate purity before faith, which then purifies and elevates the person.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says noble pre-conversion conduct shows high aspiration and freedom from vanity; the convert accepts guidance despite becoming a follower after being followed. He links insight to 20:54 and 20:128 and says faith brings illumination and duties contrary to nature."}, {"id": "90:17/q14/p3", "position": "The verse makes an organized society of mercy and justice the setting for sincere faith.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ reads the order literally: dignity through emancipation and feeding comes before faith and its communal counsels; a society tolerating enslavement and hunger cannot sustain sincere belief. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects this social reading with 107:1–2: denial of Judgment appears in turning away an orphan and failing to urge feeding the poor."}, {"id": "90:17/q14/p4", "position": "Failure to undertake the deeds and join believers shows that the moral ascent remains uncrossed.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī describes failure to thank the Benefactor; al-Iṣlāḥī says the person has not overcome the barrier to moral and spiritual growth."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q15", "question": "How does patience and mercy echo the rest of this sura?", "turns_on": "Whether the close is read as integral thematic development or, in Corpus Coranicum, a secondary stanza.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q15/p1", "position": "The sura's toil, parenthood, persecution, ascent, slavery, hunger, and poverty all call for patience and mercy.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī relates the parent and child oath to the patience of raising and protecting children; the Prophet's Meccan abuse to patience; and his mercy at the conquest to the city's reference. The boastful spender, enslaved person, famine, orphan and destitute person call for compassion. He finds five threads: toil, breadth of meaning, collective action, patience and mercy."}, {"id": "90:17/q15/p2", "position": "The verse extends the sura's collective pattern.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī connects parents and offspring, paired faculties and paths, multiple ascent duties, mutual advice and the gathered unbelievers; he says 'labad' contributes to the same pattern, unlike a plain word for many, comparing 80:20 and 76:3."}, {"id": "90:17/q15/p3", "position": "The close shifts the ethical demand into the opposed destinies of saved and damned.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls 17–20 probably secondary: it extends the ethical demand into group identities amid conflict around Muhammad, continues the rhyme of 11–16 and completes a chiastic 4+6+6+4 pattern."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q16", "question": "How does this verse relate to Sūrat al-ʿAṣr and other passages?", "turns_on": "Which neighboring or parallel passage is being used to explain the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q16/p1", "position": "It resembles 103:3 in joining faith with mutual exhortation.", "reasons": "Corpus Coranicum calls 103:3 likely secondary. Al-Iṣlāḥī and Study Quran connect perseverance here with 103:1–3. Al-Sāmarrāʾī says al-ʿAṣr begins with truth because its loss is general and truth directs patience; al-Balad focuses on one part of truth, mercy and feeding, so its patience comes first."}, {"id": "90:17/q16/p2", "position": "The sura answers the neglect of orphans and poor condemned in al-Fajr.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī contrasts al-Fajr 89:15–18's rich and poor and condemnation of neglect with al-Balad's expenditure, poverty and commanded feeding."}, {"id": "90:17/q16/p3", "position": "It anticipates the people of the right in the following verse.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī links belief, counsel, emancipation and feeding to blessing, happiness and right-hand records; Ibn al-Jawzī points to 56:7–8 and 10:46, while al-Qurṭubī records explanations involving right-side records, felicity, Adam's right side and a right-side station before summing them as Paradise's people."}, {"id": "90:17/q16/p4", "position": "The description of believers leads to the promise for the people of the right.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says naming believers prepares both praise of their mutual counsel and the glad tidings in the next verse."}, {"id": "90:17/q16/p5", "position": "It parallels Sūrat al-Māʿūn: denial of Judgment shows in repelling an orphan and failing to urge feeding the poor.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ cites 107:1–2 to support her reading that emancipation and compassion precede genuine faith."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q17", "question": "What do the pre-Islamic good-deed reports say about this verse?", "turns_on": "The cited reports distinguish earlier good carried into conversion from earlier good without faith at death.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q17/p1", "position": "The Prophet told Ḥakīm ibn Ḥizām that he entered Islam with good already done.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī, al-Rāzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Biqāʿī, Ibn ʿĀshūr and Kur'an Yolu cite his question about earlier charity, manumission and kinship. Ibn ʿĀshūr calls the report sound, glosses ḥinath as worship and says the old deeds receive reward as though done in Islam; al-Biqāʿī's full note phrases the Prophet's saying in the first person."}, {"id": "90:17/q17/p2", "position": "The Prophet said Ibn Judʿān's earlier generosity would not benefit him because he never sought forgiveness for Judgment Day.", "reasons": "ʿĀʾisha asks about his care for relatives and needy people, hospitality, feeding, emancipation and freeing captives. Al-Qurṭubī and Ibn ʿĀshūr use the reply when discussing deeds without faith."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q18", "question": "Which Prophetic sayings support the call to mercy?", "turns_on": "Which specific Prophetic formulation is cited.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q18/p1", "position": "The Merciful shows mercy to those who show mercy on earth.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and Study Quran cite the instruction to show mercy to those on earth so those above show mercy; Ibn Kathīr's full account attributes it to the Prophet."}, {"id": "90:17/q18/p2", "position": "God does not show mercy to one who does not show mercy to people.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr and al-Bursawī cite this second saying."}, {"id": "90:17/q18/p3", "position": "One who lacks mercy for the young and respect for elders is not of the community.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Abū Dāwūd transmits this from ʿAbd Allāh ibn ʿAmr; his full account attributes the saying to the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q19", "question": "What does the report about Islam and faith say?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q19/p1", "position": "The Prophet defined Islam by patience and generosity, and faith by good speech and feeding.", "reasons": "Tustarī also identifies the best speech as remembrance of God."}]}

{"id": "90:17/q21", "question": "How do inward readings understand the obstacle and its virtues?", "turns_on": "Which inner difficulty is called the obstacle.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q21/p1", "position": "The obstacle is the self: liberate it from servitude to creatures and occupy it in worship of God.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports al-Qāsim's inward gloss."}, {"id": "90:17/q21/p2", "position": "The afterlife obstacle demands restraint from forbidden and doubtful food, taking only what preserves life.", "reasons": "Al-Bursawī reports al-Muḥāsibī's teaching."}, {"id": "90:17/q21/p3", "position": "The ascent of faith purifies the mind and frees it from vanity before patience and mercy complete character.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reads earlier noble traits as preparation, faith as intellectual purification and courage and mercy as successive moral passes."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q22", "question": "What additional points are made about the poem cited for thumma?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q22/p1", "position": "Its 'then' can order words without necessarily placing whole clauses later in time.", "reasons": "The Ḥamāsa commentator applies this directly to 90:17 and to 90:12–16, saying faith is not postponed until after the listed deeds. The poem praises courage in deadly danger; 'son of a free woman' invokes pure ancestry, ghamāʾ denotes covering, ghawāshī refers to sword grips or scabbards versus blades, qisma stands for muqāsama, and sharr is an accusative verbal noun."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q23", "question": "What does the cited grammar discussion say about kāna and sequence elsewhere?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q23/p1", "position": "The cited uses can express continuing divine attributes or a relation ordered without simple elapsed time.", "reasons": "Al-Itqān records the difficulty that a past-tense 'was merciful' could imply mercy before recipients or its absence now. It reports a conjunction reading, order of report, sequence between two creations, khalaqa meaning 'decreed,' al-Kirmānī's continuing attributes whose effects occur by will, and Ibn ʿAbbās's kāna as permanence."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q24", "question": "What virtue is reported for reciting Sūrat al-Balad?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q24/p1", "position": "A report promises safety from God's anger on Judgment Day to its reciter.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf's full account transmits this promise from the Prophet."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q25", "question": "What does the visiting orator report say about believers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q25/p1", "position": "Thābit ibn Qays praised the believers' early faith and pledged the Anṣār's protection and struggle.", "reasons": "Ibn Hishām reports that, at the Prophet's instruction, Thābit answered a visiting orator by praising God, the Prophet, the Quran, the Muhājirūn and Anṣār, and committed the Anṣār to defend believers and fight unbelievers until they believe."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q26", "question": "What forms of mercy fit the believers' conduct?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q26/p1", "position": "Mercy should be cultivated in ways suited to time and place, with love and aversion for God's sake.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says believers cultivate great mercy and orient themselves toward what brings divine love; his fuller account pairs this with faith's purification from ostentation and self-admiration."}]}
{"id": "90:17/q27", "question": "How do earlier descriptions of the destitute illuminate the call to mercy?", "turns_on": "Which concrete image of complete destitution explains the earlier feeding duty.", "positions": [{"id": "90:17/q27/p1", "position": "The miskīn of the ascent can be utterly dirt-bound and perhaps poorer than a faqīr.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya describes someone thrown onto bare earth and stuck to dirt, making the need addressed by feeding especially acute."}, {"id": "90:17/q27/p2", "position": "He can be homeless, sitting on the roadside dirt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Sufyān's description."}, {"id": "90:17/q27/p3", "position": "He can return to a home containing nothing but dirt.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports Ibn ʿAbbās's description."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q01", "question": "What does the night signify here?", "turns_on": "Whether the night is read as the physical phenomenon, the natural self, or an inward cosmic experience.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q01/p1", "position": "The actual recurring night, marked by darkness, obscurity, and concealment.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says it gradually obscures what daylight showed and suits secrecy; Elmalılı allows the whole class of nights, and says its darkness follows existing light rather than primordial nonexistence. He also allows a particular terrifying night, literally or figuratively. Al-Biqāʿī adds that night brings confusion and ambiguity to people's circumstances, and that its gradual concealment displays its Creator's majesty and power to efface and bring forth. Ibn ʿĀshūr says night envelops the earth and its creatures in darkness."}, {"id": "92:1/q01/p2", "position": "The natural self.", "reasons": "This is Sahl al-Tustarī's inward reading."}, {"id": "92:1/q01/p3", "position": "Cosmic and inward darkness that overwhelms perception and may bring the soul from multiplicity into annihilating unity.", "reasons": "Elmalılı describes movement from differentiation to unity, multiplicity to solitude, and witnessing to annihilation; he relates passing away to 55:26–27 and 28:88 and an ensuing abiding witness."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q02", "question": "What does the definite article in ٱلَّيْلِ specify?", "turns_on": "Whether the article denotes the class or a specific night.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q02/p1", "position": "The whole kind of night.", "reasons": "Elmalılı offers generic reference."}, {"id": "92:1/q02/p2", "position": "A particular terrifying night, literally or figuratively.", "reasons": "Elmalılı offers particular reference."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q03", "question": "What does يَغْشَىٰ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the phrase is glossed by covering and concealment or by its resulting darkness.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q03/p1", "position": "It covers, veils, or enshrouds, so darkness conceals what was visible.", "reasons": "Ibn Jubayr and Saʿīd ibn Jubayr explain covering and concealment; Qatādah describes creatures encompassed and filled. Al-Naḥḥās compares darkness to a garment and cites al-Nābigha's poem of night pursuing and catching a fugitive. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces gh-sh-y through veils, sleep, fainting, dulled sight and insight, rejection in 71:7 and 11:5, the lote tree in 53:16, coverings of senses in 3:154, 8:11, 33:19, 47:20, 2:7 and 45:23, and judgment or punishment in 88:1, 44:10–11, 29:55, 14:50 and 7:41. She notes terror and darkness in 24:40, 10:27, 31:32, 20:78, 13:3, 7:54 and 91:4, and understands this night as deep darkness. Al-Jishumī contrasts ghishāʾ, covering, with tajallī, clarity and illumination. Al-Durr reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's gloss that night approaches and covers everything. Al-Biqāʿī emphasizes that the covering gradually hides what daylight showed."}, {"id": "92:1/q03/p2", "position": "It means that night darkens.", "reasons": "Mujāhid gives this concise gloss; the physical effect is the night removing daylight's light. Al-Dāmghānī compares the sense 'become dark' with 91:4; al-Durr reports the same gloss from Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q04", "question": "What does the night cover?", "turns_on": "Which implicit object is supplied for the verb, or how broadly its covering is understood.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q04/p1", "position": "The day or daylight.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī says night removes daylight's light until day clears and reveals what was hidden; al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī cite 13:3; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān cite 7:54; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī cites 13:3; al-Qummī also calls this an oath. Elmalılı includes daylight among the possible objects. Al-Ṭabarī and al-Baghawī say night removes the day's light; al-Ṭabarī adds that the next day reveals what night concealed. Al-Rāzī also cites 7:54 for the day as object."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p2", "position": "The sun.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī invoke 91:4; al-Nasafī points to the sun in the preceding oath; Abū Ḥayyān and Elmalılı likewise connect the possibility with 91:4. Al-Ālūsī says the sworn object is the entire night whichever object is supplied. Al-Kashshāf, al-Rāzī and al-Nasafī support the sun as object by 91:4."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p3", "position": "Everything hidden by darkness, including all creatures or all creation.", "reasons": "Qatādah says night encompasses and fills all creatures. Al-Kashshāf and al-Rāzī cite 113:3; al-Nasafī cites the nightfall verse 113:3. Al-Ālūsī says the object may be whatever night veils in general, while the oath is by the whole night. Ibn ʿĀshūr makes universal coverage the lesson of the intransitive use. Al-Qurṭubī separately reports creatures and everything covered by darkness. Ibn Kathīr describes creation as covered in darkness; al-Durr reports Saʿīd ibn Jubayr's 'everything' gloss."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p4", "position": "The earth and what is on it.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī gives earth as one possible object; Abū Ḥayyān says earth and all it contains; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Study Quran also offer earth. Ibn ʿAṭiyya explicitly names the earth and everything in it; Ibn ʿĀshūr says night envelops the earth and its creatures."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p5", "position": "The horizons, or the horizon and everything between heaven and earth.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī specifies the horizon under darkness; Ibn al-Jawzī reports al-Zajjāj's wider horizon-to-earth account; Elmalılı includes all horizons."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p6", "position": "The world.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as a possible unexpressed object; Quṭb depicts the world as enveloped and hidden."}, {"id": "92:1/q04/p7", "position": "Grief or people's

eyes, hearts, and faculties through sleep and heedlessness.", "reasons": "Elmalılı extends the physical image to affect and perception, citing 6:60."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q05", "question": "Why is the object of يَغْشَىٰ left unexpressed?", "turns_on": "Whether the missing object is recoverable, intentionally left wide, or absent because the verb is used intransitively.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q05/p1", "position": "The listener can infer the object from context.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās and al-Qurṭubī say it is understood; al-Nasafī takes the preceding mention of the sun as contextual evidence, citing 91:4."}, {"id": "92:1/q05/p2", "position": "Leaving it open broadens the image to every possible object.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās says the omission may deliberately leave the object vague. Elmalılı says it broadens the meaning and heightens terror, while pointing back to 91:4; al-Sāmarrāʾī says it keeps all possible objects in view."}, {"id": "92:1/q05/p3", "position": "The verb functions intransitively here to teach that night covers everything.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr explicitly explains the omission as intransitive use and draws the universal lesson."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q06", "question": "How does إِذَا describe the time of the covering?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q06/p1", "position": "It presents the covering as a realized event that may occur now or later.", "reasons": "Elmalılı says conditional idhā asserts realization and the imperfect verb can indicate present or future time."}, {"id": "92:1/q06/p2", "position": "إِذَا is purely temporal in the oath and does not make the oath conditional.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī argues that a conditional reading would make the oath take place only when night fades, whereas the oath is made unconditionally now."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q07", "question": "How is the case of إِذَا governed in the coordinated oaths?", "turns_on": "Whether the coordinating wāws themselves must govern two cases, or coordination joins paired constituents under the first oath governor.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q07/p1", "position": "The construction poses a governance difficulty: coordination appears to make the wāws govern both genitive and accusative, or the oath wāws create a disputed construction.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān reports al-Zamakhsharī's account and objects that coordinating wāws are not themselves governors; he says al-Zamakhsharī merely calls the disputed construction disliked where al-Khalīl's wording prohibits it."}, {"id": "92:1/q07/p2", "position": "The later wāws coordinate genitive-and-accusative pairs; the first oath particle supplies governance rather than each coordinating wāw governing two cases.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān gives مررت بزيد أمس وعمرو اليوم as a parallel and cites Sībawayh's poetic coordination of a genitive and nominative in the same pattern. He reports al-Khalīl that the first wāw acts like oath bāʾ or tāʾ, while the later wāws join nouns by ordinary coordination; he reads al-Khalīl as prohibiting the competing account."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q08", "question": "Why is يَغْشَىٰ imperfect while the following daylight verb is perfect?", "turns_on": "Whether the tense contrast chiefly depicts the different pace of night and day or creates immediate presence through a past form.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q08/p1", "position": "Night's covering unfolds gradually, whereas daylight appears at once at sunrise.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī compares the paired verbs in al-Shams, 91:3–4; he explains the imperfect for the continuing covering and the perfect for sudden manifestation."}, {"id": "92:1/q08/p2", "position": "A past form can make a present event vivid and immediate by placing the listener at the event.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī explains that Arabic past verbs have more temporal uses than simple past reference; he illustrates the shift with the Prophet turning toward heaven in 2:144 and the reproach for killing prophets in 3:21."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q09", "question": "Why is yaghshā apt here while 93:2 uses sajā?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q09/p1", "position": "Yaghshā suggests movement and covering; sajā gives both stillness and darkness suited to the pause in revelation.", "reasons": "Al-Sāmarrāʾī says sajā fits revelation's suspension and loss of light, whereas yaghshā and yasrī imply movement; he compares 92:1 and 89:4."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q10", "question": "How do night and day function in creation and human life?", "turns_on": "Which aspect of the paired phenomena carries the argument: daily benefit, divine governance, human divergence, the Hereafter, or secrecy.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q10/p1", "position": "They alternate as divine signs and provide complementary times for shelter, sleep, activity, and livelihood.", "reasons": "Qatādah calls them two great signs God rotates over creation. Al-Rāzī describes animals sheltered and creatures stilled for restorative sleep, then people, birds and other creatures moving for livelihood, citing 25:62 and 14:33. Abū Ḥayyān contrasts creatures' night shelter with daytime dispersal. Quṭb stresses their opposed appearance, qualities, effects, and recurring cycle. Al-Rāzī calls sleep rest for bodies and nourishment for spirits, and says perpetual night would prevent livelihood while perpetual day would remove rest; he cites 25:62 and 14:33. He also mentions birds leaving nests and vermin leaving hiding places in daylight."}, {"id": "92:1/q10/p2", "position": "Their precise alternation points to a power governing the cosmos and purposeful human life.", "reasons": "Quṭb says the broad change touches the soul, evokes human inability to control the mysterious universe, and shows another hand ordering the heavens and directing lives; instinct and reflection recognize this director even amid denial. Küran Yolu sees the worth of creatures and greatness of their Creator in the oaths. Al-Biqāʿī reads the gradual covering as a sign of God's power to efface and bring forth and of His voluntary direction of souls. Ibn ʿĀshūr finds signs of divine power and fine workmanship in the ordered night and day, referring to 91:3–4."}, {"id": "92:1/q10/p3", "position": "Their contrast provides a cosmic frame or matrix for divergent human deeds and recompense.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr pairs night darkness and day brightness with the created male and female, citing 78:8 and 51:49. Quṭb relates the two opposed outcomes to night/day and male/female. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ traces the contrast to fire for the denier and satisfaction for the pious giver. Corpus Coranicum says the two cosmic oppositions frame varied human aims and their recompense, with God later speaking in 92:7–10; Neuwirth calls the elemental pairs a structural matrix. Study Quran likewise links the polarity with opposed ends of deeds. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the contrast fits believers' and unbelievers' different conditions in this life and the next, while al-Durr reports Ibn ʿAbbās that the surah concerns generosity and miserliness."}, {"id": "92:1/q10/p4", "position": "Their complementary pairing argues that creation has a completing counterpart, ultimately the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī says night/day and male/female fill one another's void, making their capacities and purpose intelligible; their harmony argues for monotheism and judgment, with 51:49 as a reminder. He says outer and inner evidence in 92:1–4 establishes the need for the Hereafter as this world's counterpart."}, {"id": "92:1/q10/p5", "position": "Night suits concealment and day publicity, whatever the moral quality of an act.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the righteous and wicked alike choose night for secrecy and day for publicity. Al-Biqāʿī says night conceals secrets, joins the good and separates the wicked."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q11", "question": "What is the oath by the night doing?", "turns_on": "Whether the note explains the oath's argumentative function or its proposed literary antecedent.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q11/p1", "position": "It invokes a natural sign to establish the ensuing premise and direct attention to the surah's subject.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī identifies the oath; Iṣlāḥī says Qurʾānic oaths by natural phenomena establish a premise. {"id": "92:1/q14", "question": "What further inward or ominous meaning can the night's covering bear?", "turns_on": "Which extended spiritual or eschatological effect is drawn from the covering image.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q14/p1", "position": "Night prayer and good deeds can turn spiritual light into sensory light after death.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī reports this from some interpreters."}, {"id": "92:1/q14/p2", "position": "Its engulfing darkness can warn of punishment, ignorance, death agonies, or resurrection events.", "reasons": "Elmalılı offers a town or people engulfed by punishment, the age of ignorance around the Prophet's mission, death agonies, and resurrection scenes as possible images."}, {"id": "92:1/q14/p3", "position": "It can signify passing away of existent things before abiding witness to God.", "reasons": "Elmalılı distinguishes this accidental darkness from primordial nonexistence, cites 55:26–27 and 28:88 on all perishing except God's face, and describes movement from annihilation to abiding witness."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q15", "question": "What was the surah's place and period of revelation?", "turns_on": "Whether the whole surah belongs to Mecca, Medina, or both; the notes also differ in confidence about the Meccan attribution.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q15/p1", "position": "It is Meccan, with Study Quran calling it early Meccan and often ninth in revelation order.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī calls the Meccan attribution a consensus; Abū Ḥayyān reports it as his own view. {"id": "92:1/q17", "question": "Why is the surah named al-Layl?", "turns_on": "Whether the explanation identifies the naming source or the significance al-Biqāʿī finds in it.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q17/p1", "position": "It is named after its opening oath by night.", "reasons": "Study Quran states the naming basis."}, {"id": "92:1/q17/p2", "position": "The name signals night as frustration of ordinary desire through darkness and sleep, the sibling of death.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī explains the name's thematic force."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q18", "question": "What event occasioned the surah's revelation?", "turns_on": "Which charitable act is connected with revelation and how the palm narrative's chain is assessed.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q18/p1", "position": "A believer acquired a palm from a stingy owner and gave it to a deprived household.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim's Ibn ʿAbbās report says fallen dates were withheld, the buyer traded forty palms for the tree, and a palm in Paradise was promised. Ibn Kathīr's Ibn ʿAbbās version adds that the owner snatched fruit from poor children, refused the Prophet's offer of a palm in Paradise, and another man donated the purchased tree; Ibn Kathīr says the story explains the opening contrast of giving and withholding. Al-Ālūsī identifies the buyer in al-Suddī's version as Abū al-Daḥdāḥ and the beneficiaries as orphans, but reports al-Suyūṭī's judgment that the Ibn ʿAbbās report is weak; Ibn Kathīr calls Ibn Abī Ḥātim's report very unusual. Al-Baghawī reports ʿAṭāʾ's version: Abū al-Daḥdāḥ exchanged his garden for the owner's palm and gave it to the neighbor; the giver and miser exemplify 92:5–10. Al-Durr calls the Ibn ʿAbbās version weak in chain and says the buyer traded forty palms. Ibn ʿĀshūr says this occasion for 92:5 underlies some Medinan attributions."}, {"id": "92:1/q18/p2", "position": "It concerned Abū Bakr's charitable action, including his purchase and freeing of Bilāl.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says most reports concern Abū Bakr, citing sound chains from Ibn Masʿūd, Ibn ʿAbbās and others. Ibn Masʿūd reports that Abū Bakr bought Bilāl from Umayya ibn Khalaf for a cloak and ten uqiyyas and freed him, after which the opening was revealed. Al-Rāzī reports al-Qaffāl that the surah concerns Abū Bakr's spending on Muslims against Umayya ibn Khalaf's miserliness and disbelief. Al-Ālūsī says most reports support an Abū Bakr occasion with sound chains and that some commentators identify him with the most God-fearing in 92:17, some claiming consensus."}, {"id": "92:1/q18/p3", "position": "Some Shiʿite interpreters assign the passage about the most God-fearing in 92:17 to ʿAlī.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports this attribution alongside the Abū Bakr attribution for that passage."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q19", "question": "What reward is reported for reciting this surah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q19/p1", "position": "The reciter receives until contentment, is protected from hardship, and has ease made easy.", "reasons": "Al-Jishumī transmits this as a prophetic report from Ubayy."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q20", "question": "What recitation of al-Layl did the Prophet direct in prayer?", "turns_on": "The reports describe different instructions and prayer settings.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q20/p1", "position": "Muʿādh was told to use shorter chapters, among them al-Layl, instead of prolonging prayer.", "reasons": "Al-Durr reports the Prophet's rebuke and his examples of chapters beginning with glorification, sun, dawn and night, mentioning 87:1, 91:1 and 92:1. {"id": "92:1/q21", "question": "How were the endings such as يَغْشَىٰ read?", "turns_on": "The transmitted degree and distribution of imālah across the sūrah endings.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q21/p1", "position": "With open vowels, without imālah.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī reports this for Ibn Kathīr, ʿĀṣim and Ibn ʿĀmir across the relevant endings of al-Layl and al-Ḍuḥā; some Nāfiʿ transmissions through Warsh and Qālūn also open them all."}, {"id": "92:1/q21/p2", "position": "With full imālah of the endings.", "reasons": "Al-Fārisī reports this throughout for al-Kisāʾī; ʿAbbās transmits fully inclined forms from Abū ʿAmr for selected endings."}, {"id": "92:1/q21/p3", "position": "With intermediate imālah.", "reasons": "Some Nāfiʿ transmissions give an intermediate pronunciation, and Abū ʿAmr is also reported to use intermediate imālah."}, {"id": "92:1/q21/p4", "position": "With selective opening or inclination depending on the ending.", "reasons": "Another Nāfiʿ report opens only talāhā and inclines the rest; al-Fārisī records differing Abū ʿAmr transmissions across verse endings, including 79:30."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q22", "question": "How was the oath's male-and-female clause read?", "turns_on": "Whether the early reported wording without mā remains the operative reading or was superseded by the agreed muṣḥaf wording.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q22/p1", "position": "It was recited as 'the male and the female' without mā.", "reasons": "Ibn Jinnī reports this from the Prophet, ʿAlī, Ibn Masʿūd, Abū al-Dardāʾ and Ibn ʿAbbās; he treats it as evidence for a variant making the pair genitive in apposition to mā. Ibn ʿĀshūr cites the two Ṣaḥīḥs' report from ʿAlqama: Abū al-Dardāʾ heard the Prophet recite Ibn Masʿūd's wording. He says al-Zamakhsharī called it the Prophet's reading, but explains it as an early permitted variant later replaced. Al-Durr reports Abū Isḥāq's account of ʿAbdallāh's connected recitation of the night and day oaths followed by 'the male and female'; Ibn ʿĀshūr reports ʿAlqama's account that Abū al-Dardāʾ testified to hearing it from the Prophet."}, {"id": "92:1/q22/p2", "position": "The final agreed reading retains mā in the clause.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says this is the reciters' agreed final reading and the form written in Abū Bakr's muṣḥaf. Ibn ʿĀshūr explains the earlier variant as an early license superseded by the Prophet's final-life reading and says the canonical readers and Abū Bakr's codex retain mā."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q23", "question": "How does this opening connect with the preceding surah?", "turns_on": "Whether the link lies in repeated oath wording, development of the moral polarity, or reversal of the prior narrative movement.", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q23/p1", "position": "It

 echoes the preceding surah's night-and-day oath wording and temporal restrictions.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr links the time restrictions to explanations of the oaths in 91:3–4. {"id": "92:1/q24", "question": "What does the paired day's tajallī mean against this night's covering?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q24/p1", "position": "It is appearing, becoming uncovered, and making things clear.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ illustrates the physical senses with a receding hairline, polish that clears sight, the display of a bride, and polishing a blade or mirror; this supplies the lexical opposite of the night’s covering. {"id": "92:1/q25", "question": "What other titles are attested for this surah?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q25/p1", "position": "Sūrat al-Layl, Sūrat wa-l-Layl, and Sūrat wa-l-Layl idhā yaghshā.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr finds al-Layl in most Qurʾān copies and some tafsīrs, wa-l-Layl in most tafsīrs, and wa-l-Layl idhā yaghshā in al-Bukhārī and al-Tirmidhī."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q26", "question": "Does the reported occasion limit the surah's meaning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q26/p1", "position": "No; its statements about differing human effort and the warning of fire apply generally.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī says the surah's general wording at 92:4 and 92:14 extends beyond the reported Abū Bakr and Umayya occasion."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q27", "question": "What formal feature do the paired night and day oaths illustrate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q27/p1", "position": "They illustrate patterned Qurʾānic verse endings.", "reasons": "Al-Zarkashī uses the pair as an example of patterned endings."}]}
{"id": "92:1/q28", "question": "What overall message does the surah develop after its opening oath?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "92:1/q28/p1", "position": "It contrasts believers' virtues and reward with unbelievers' faults and recompense, and presents God's guidance and the Messenger's warning.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says God guides and rewards people in this life and the next, while the Messenger reminds them of God and His reward; the fearful heed him and the wretched turn away toward the great fire."}]}

{"id": "93:1/q01", "question": "What does al-ḍuḥā denote in this oath?", "turns_on": "Whether the term denotes a whole day, a particular time or light, or an event or symbolic referent.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q01/p1", "position": "The whole daylight or daytime.", "reasons": "Tabari, Tha'labi, Baghawi, Tabrisi, Razi, Qurtubi, Nasafi, Kuranyolu and Shawkani appeal to its contrast with night; Baghawi, Kashshaf, Qurtubi and Alusi cite 7:98, Qurtubi also 7:97. Mujahid links it with exposure to sun. Alusi says the objection assumes an intensely dark night without proof. Bint al-Shati reports Tabari's choice of visible daylight, but cites 79:46, 20:59 and 91:1 against the whole-day sense. Al-Ṭabarī cites 20:119 for exposure to sunlight; al-Māwardī attributes this derivation to ʿAlī ibn ʿĪsā. Al-Ālūsī reports an objection based on an allegedly intense night, then denies that the qualifying phrase requires intensified darkness."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p2", "position": "A defined forenoon or midmorning after sunrise.", "reasons": "Qatada and Muqatil describe temperate heat or cold. Kashshaf, Razi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Alusi, Elmalili, Islahi and Samarrai describe the sun rising high and strong light. Alusi prefers a time over sunlight or sunrise because of the next oath. Bint al-Shati cites 79:46, 20:59 and 91:1 for a particular hour; Abduh calls it sunlight in the day's prime. Study Quran gives daybreak-to-noon as a wider range. Bint al-Shati stresses that the oath is limited to forenoon rather than daylight generally, and that its light can be weaker than at noon. Al-Ālūsī specifically distinguishes the time when the sun has appeared above the horizon from sunlight itself or the sun's height, finding the time more fitting to the following oath."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p3", "position": "The hour Moses' opponents prostrated.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Kashshaf, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Nasafi, Bursawi, Alusi and Study Quran relate it to the gathering at 20:59. Razi sees a promise that God can honor Muhammad and turn his enemies' hearts. Bint al-Shati calls the reading anachronistic because these passages came later."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p4", "position": "The beginning or first hour of day.", "reasons": "Qatada calls it an hour or the start; Suddi and Muqatil specify the sun moving onward. Jishumi derives it from appearing in sunlight. Bursawi allows metonymy for the time or an omitted noun."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p5", "position": "Sunlight, brightness, or visible exposure.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya calls it the rise and strength of light; Tabari's daylight is visible sunlight; Ibn Kathir swears by forenoon and its light. Study Quran says the title most commonly means rising sunlight and can extend to all creation it reveals. Bint al-Shati says the root centers on visibility; Wahidi and Ibn Ashur refer to the parallel at 91:1. Yaqub derives aḍḥā from sheep sacrificed at this hour. Ibn ʿĀshūr directs readers to his explanation of the term at 91:1."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p6", "position": "The morning when God spoke to Moses.", "reasons": "Tha'labi, Qushayri, Qurtubi, Baydawi, Bursawi and Study Quran report this; Ja'far pairs it with the Night Journey, citing 7:143 and 17:1. Bint al-Shati objects that the cited passages were revealed later."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p7", "position": "The forenoon prayer.", "reasons": "Qushayri lists it; Study Quran notes the term also names a late-morning supererogatory prayer."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p8", "position": "The Prophet's radiant face.", "reasons": "Bursawi cites a Persian couplet pairing it with his dark hair; Elmalili reports the association. Bint al-Shati excludes such esoteric identifications."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p9", "position": "Sunrise itself.", "reasons": "Qutrub identifies it with sunrise."}, {"id": "93:1/q01/p10", "position": "The dawn of the Muhammadan mission and truth.", "reasons": "Elmalili prefers a specific dawn of truth radiating mercy and light over a generic definite article."}]}
{"id": "93:1/q02", "question": "How is the final vowel of al-ḍuḥā written and explained?", "turns_on": "Whether spelling follows spoken form, root origin or muṣḥaf and neighboring endings.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q02/p1", "position": "Its final alif is written in yāʾ shape in the muṣḥaf despite a wāw root.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says this follows neighboring endings, mostly yāʾ-derived, supports imāla in relevant dialects, and cites Ibn Malik. {"id": "93:1/q05", "question": "Why is the forenoon singled out for an oath?", "turns_on": "Whether its sensory quality, a past event, or a divine sign supplies the point.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q05/p1", "position": "It recalls divine speech to Moses and the magicians' prostration.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Razi, Nasafi, Bursawi, Alusi and Elmalili cite 20:59 and God's ability to honor Muhammad and change his enemies. {"id": "93:1/q07", "question": "What inward or symbolic reality is signified by ḍuḥā?", "turns_on": "The different spiritual correspondences assigned to daylight.", "positions": [{"id": "93:1/q07/p1", "position": "Spirit or God's unveiling of an inner secret.", "reasons": "Tustari identifies the spirit; Ibn Ata says God unveils the secret as the servant is occupied with calling people through attention to creation."}, {"id": "93:1/q07/p2", "position": "The station of witnessing.", "reasons": "Junayd pairs it with night's inner-eye station or ghayn, clouding over the heart in a Prophetic report; Sulami and Bursawi transmit related forms."}, {"id": "93:1/q07/p3", "position": "The Prophet's radiant face.", "reasons": "Bursawi's Persian couplet pairs face with hair.
